questions.question: What is the supremum of a set $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}$?
options: The greatest lower bound of $E$.
Any element of $E$.
The least upper bound of $E$.
The smallest element of $E$ only when it belongs to $E$.

questions.question: Which set has supremum $1$ but no maximum?
What is $\sup(0,1)$?
options: It does not exist because $1\notin(0,1)$.

questions.question: What is the supremum of $\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon x \lt 2\}$?
options: No supremum exists.

questions.question: Must the supremum of a set be an element of that set?
options: A supremum must always be an element of the set.
A supremum can never be an upper bound.
A supremum need not belong to the set.
A supremum is always smaller than every element of the set.

questions.question: Does $E=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon x>0\}$ have a supremum in $\mathbb{R}$?
options: No; it is not bounded above.
Yes; $\sup E=0$
Yes; $\sup E=1$
Yes; $\sup E$ is a finite real number

questions.question: Why is the phrase least upper bound more precise than simply upper bound?
options: There may be many upper bounds, but the supremum is the smallest one.
There is only ever one upper bound, so the word 'least' adds nothing.
The least upper bound must belong to the set, unlike other upper bounds.
There may be many upper bounds, and the supremum is the largest of them.

questions.question: Which statement uses the existence theorem without dropping an assumption?
options: A non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a supremum.
Every set of real numbers has a supremum.
Every bounded-below set of real numbers has a supremum.
Every set with no elements has a supremum by this theorem.

questions.question: For $E = (0,1)$, why is $1$ the supremum rather than a maximum?
options: $1$ is smaller than every element of $E$.
$1$ is the least upper bound, but $1\notin E$.
$1$ is not an upper bound of $E$.
$1$ belongs to $E$ and is its largest element.

questions.question: Let $E = \{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon x\leq 2\}$. What is $\sup E$, and is it attained?
options: $\sup E = 2$, but a supremum can never belong to the set.
$\sup E = 2$, and in this case the supremum belongs to $E$.
$\sup E = 1$ because $2$ is an endpoint.
$E$ has no supremum because it has infinitely many elements.

questions.question: Which two properties characterise $s=\sup E$?
options: $s$ is the least upper bound of $E$.
$s\in E$ and $s$ is the largest element of $E$
$s$ is a lower bound and it is the largest such
$s$ is simply some upper bound of $E$

questions.question: If $s=\sup E$, what does every choice of $\varepsilon>0$ guarantee?
options: Some element of $E$ is greater than $s-\varepsilon$
Every element of $E$ is greater than $s-\varepsilon$
$s-\varepsilon$ belongs to $E$
$E$ must be finite

questions.question: When it exists, how many suprema can a set have?
options: Exactly two.
At most one.
Infinitely many.
One for each element of the set.

questions.question: What is the supremum of a non-empty finite set of real numbers?
options: Its largest element
Its smallest element
Its average
It has no supremum

questions.question: How does a supremum differ from a maximum?
options: A supremum must belong to the set, while a maximum need not.
A supremum is always a lower bound.
A maximum must belong to the set, while a supremum need not.
A maximum is never an upper bound.
